1.note: In some translations this verse appears at the end of chapter 28 and other translations, at the beginning of chapter 29. You may wish to follow the convention of a locally accepted translation. This reflects that this verse could (1) look ahead to everything in chapter 29. Use a natural form in your language that indicates that it applies to what follows such as ending punctuation. Alternate translation: [These are the words of … at Horeb:] or (2) refer back to everything in chapter 28. Alternate translation: [Those were the words of … at Horeb]

1.q: הַ⁠בְּרִ֜ית אֲֽשֶׁר־צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֣ה אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֗ה לִ⁠כְרֹ֛ת אֶת־בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל
1.note: Moses is using **cut** and **covenant** as part of a common expression of his culture, “to cut a covenant,” which means “to make” or “establish” a covenant. See how you translated the phrase “cut a covenant” in 5:2. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the covenant that Yahweh commanded Moses to make with the sons of Israel] or [the covenant that Yahweh commanded Moses to establish with the sons of Israel]

Here, **sons** means “descendants.” Moses is identifying the Israelites as descendants of their ancestor Jacob, who was also known as Israel. See how you translated the phrase “sons of Israel” in 4:44. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the descendants of Israel] or [with the Israelites]
See how you translated the similar expression using “covenant” and “cut with” in the first phrase of this verse. Alternate translation: [the covenant that he had made with them]
**Horeb** is the name of a mountain that is also known as Mount Sinai. You could add a footnote to show that this refers to the events described in Exodus 32.

2.note: Here the word **Israel** represents the people of the nation of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or plain language. Alternate translation: [to all the Israelites]

The term **and said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.
See how you translated the phrase “before your eyes” in 1:30. Alternate translation: [in your sight]

3.note: Moses is using one part of a person, the **eyes**, to mean all of the person in the act of seeing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that you saw]

4.note: See how you translated the phrase “until this day” in 2:22. Alternate translation: [until this present time]

4.q: לָ⁠כֶ֥ם לֵב֙ לָ⁠דַ֔עַת וְ⁠עֵינַ֥יִם לִ⁠רְא֖וֹת וְ⁠אָזְנַ֣יִם לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֑עַ
4.note: Here, **a heart to know or eyes to see or ears to hear** represents the ability to understand and comprehend all that someone sees or hears. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you understanding of all you see and hear]

4.q: לֵב֙ לָ⁠דַ֔עַת וְ⁠עֵינַ֥יִם לִ⁠רְא֖וֹת וְ⁠אָזְנַ֣יִם לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֑עַ
4.note: These three phrases **a heart to know** and **eyes to see** and **ears to hear** mean basically the same thing. The second and third emphasize the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including all three phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could combine the phrases in a way that shows that the second and third phrases are repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [understanding all that you see and hear]

5.q: וָ⁠אוֹלֵ֥ךְ אֶתְ⁠כֶ֛ם & כִּ֛י אֲנִ֥י יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵי⁠כֶֽם
5.note: In verses 5–6 there is a shift of who is speaking. It seems that Moses directly quotes Yahweh. You may choose to mark these verses as a second level direct quotation or change it to refer to Yahweh indirectly. Alternate translation: [And he has lead you … that Yahweh is your God.]
This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [He said, ‘And I have led]

The word **you** in **your sandals** and **your feet** is singular, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. In **led you**, **your clothes**, and **on you** they are plural.

6.note: See how you translated the phrase “Yahweh your God” in 1:10.

7.note: Here, **struck them down** represents defeating them in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we conquered them]

9.q: וּ⁠שְׁמַרְתֶּ֗ם אֶת־דִּבְרֵי֙ הַ⁠בְּרִ֣ית הַ⁠זֹּ֔את וַ⁠עֲשִׂיתֶ֖ם אֹתָ֑⁠ם
9.note: The terms **keep** and **do** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And you shall carefully obey this covenant]

10.note: Here, **to the face of** represents being in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh] or [in the presence of Yahweh]

10.q: רָאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֣ם שִׁבְטֵי⁠כֶ֗ם זִקְנֵי⁠כֶם֙ וְ⁠שֹׁ֣טְרֵי⁠כֶ֔ם כֹּ֖ל אִ֥ישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
10.note: Moses uses a repetitive series of clauses from here through the next verse to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive.

11.note: The author is referring to all kinds of labor performed by foreigners among them by naming two specific types of work, **cuts your wood** and **draws your water**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [including those who do all kinds of work for you]
The word **you** and the last two words **your** are singular here, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

12.note: Here Moses is speaking of being part of a covenant as if it were **entering into** a physical location. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to join the covenant of] or [to become part of the covenant of]
See how you translated the similar expression “to cut” as it relates to “the covenant” in [verse 1](ta:29).

13.note: Here Moses is speaking of God establishing the Israelites as his covenant people as if he would **raise** them **up** physically to a high place. This image suggests that God established them in a position of honor and distinction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he may establish you today as a people]
Here Moses is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

14.note: See how you translated the similar expression “to cut” as it relates to “the covenant” in [verse 1](ta:29).

15.q: וְ⁠אֵ֨ת אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֵינֶ֛⁠נּוּ פֹּ֖ה עִמָּ֥⁠נוּ הַ⁠יּֽוֹם
15.note: The implication is that Moses is referring to the future descendants of the Israelites who are present. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and with our future generations]

17.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the abominable things they did] or [their disgusting practices]

18.note: Moses is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the Israelites an instruction to follow in verse 9. They should “keep the words of this covenant” so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [so that there will not be among you a man]

Here, **a man or woman or clan or tribe** represents people in general at every level of society, not specific individuals or groups. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any person or family or tribal group] or [anyone at any level of your community]

18.q: אֲשֶׁר֩ לְבָב֨⁠וֹ פֹנֶ֤ה הַ⁠יּוֹם֙ מֵ⁠עִם֙ יְהוָ֣ה
18.note: Moses uses the **heart** to represent where a person’s will and emotions exist. He is speaking of disobeying Yahweh as if one **is turning away** from walking on a path that follows Yahweh. You may have comparable expressions in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who decides today to disobey Yahweh]

Moses is continuing to describe the undesired outcome of not keeping his covenant introduced at the beginning of this verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [so that there will not be among you]

Here Moses is speaking of a person who disobeys Yahweh as if that person were **a root bearing gall and wormwood**. This image emphasizes how such a person will produce bitter and harmful consequences for the community. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a person who brings trouble and bitterness]

The terms **gall** and **wormwood** are kinds of bitter plants. If your readers would not be familiar with what gall and wormwood are, you could use the names of similar plants that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [bitter and poisonous plants]

19.note: The word **himself** is used here to indicate that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. The person who blesses and the person who receives the blessing are the same individual. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same person fills two roles in the sentence.

Moses is using **bless himself in his heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “congratulate himself” or “think that he will be safe.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then he will tell himself that he will be fine] or [then he will convince himself that nothing bad will happen to him]
The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

19.q: שָׁל֣וֹם יִֽהְיֶה־לִּ֔⁠י כִּ֛י בִּ⁠שְׁרִר֥וּת לִבִּ֖⁠י אֵלֵ֑ךְ
19.note: Here this person is speaking of living as if it were literally **walking**. He also uses **heart** to refer to where one’s stubborn desires exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will have peace, though I live according to the stubbornness of my heart] or [I will have peace, though I follow my stubborn desires]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **stubbornness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [even though I stubbornly insist on doing what I want]

Here Moses is speaking of people as if they were **wet** and **dry** land. Surprisingly, both the dry (wicked) and the wet (righteous) will be swept away even though typically only dry things can be swept easily. He uses **swept away** as an image that means that everyone will be destroyed, both the righteous and the wicked. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everyone is destroyed together] or [all people are swept away]

The expression **are swept away** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will sweep away the wet and the dry]

20.note: The phrase **the nose of Yahweh … will smolder** is a common expression that means that Yahweh is very angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, in his jealousy, will be very angry with that man]

The phrase **the nose of Yahweh and his jealousy** expresses a single idea. The word **jealousy** tells more about **nose**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s jealous anger will smolder against that man]

20.q: וְ⁠רָ֤בְצָה בּ⁠וֹ֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠אָלָ֔ה הַ⁠כְּתוּבָ֖ה בַּ⁠סֵּ֣פֶר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה
20.note: Here Moses is speaking as if the curses were objects that could physically **rest on** a person. He means that the curses will affect that person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and all the curses written in this book will affect him] or [and all the curses written in this book will happen to him]

The expression **written in this book** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses. Alternate translation: [that I have written in this book]

Here Moses is speaking as if Yahweh would literally **wipe out** someone’s name the way a person might erase writing. Moses means that Yahweh will completely destroy that person so that no one will remember him. See how you translated the similar expression “wipe out their name from under the heavens” in 9:14. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will completely destroy him so he will be forgotten]

21.note: The expression **written in this book of the law** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses. Alternate translation: [that I wrote in this book of the law]

22.note: Here Moses is speaking of future generations being born as if they were people who would literally **rise up** from the ground. He means the children who will be born in future generations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your children who will be born after you] or [the generation of those who are not yet born]

23.note: Here, **All its land** is an overstatement for emphasis. The land is not literally **sulfur and burning salt** but there is so much that nothing will grow. Covering the land with sulfur and salt would poison the land and make it unusable for growing anything on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Its land is poisoned with sulfur and burning salt]

Here the terms **nose** and **wrath** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [in his great anger]

Here, **in his nose** refers to part of a common expression of this culture, “the burning of his nose” which means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in his anger]

24.note: The author is using **the heat of this great nose** as a common expression of his culture to mean “this great anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What is this great anger] or [What is this fierce wrath]

25.q: אֶת־בְּרִ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם אֲשֶׁר֙ כָּרַ֣ת עִמָּ֔⁠ם
25.note: Moses is using **covenant** and **cut** as part of a common expression of his culture, “to cut a covenant,” which means “to make” or “establish” a covenant. See how you translated the phrase “cut a covenant” in 5:2. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the covenant that Yahweh established with their fathers]

26.note: Here Moses is speaking as if these gods were something the people could have a **portion of**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and that they never belonged to]

27.note: See how you translated the similar phrase “the nose of Yahweh your God burn” in 6:15.

27.q: לְ⁠הָבִ֤יא עָלֶ֨י⁠הָ֙ אֶת־כָּל־הַ⁠קְּלָלָ֔ה הַ⁠כְּתוּבָ֖ה בַּ⁠סֵּ֥פֶר הַ⁠זֶּֽה
27.note: The expression **all the curses written in this book** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses. Alternate translation: [all the curses that Moses wrote in this book]

28.note: Here the author is speaking as if Yahweh had literally **torn** the Israelites away from their land, as someone might tear a piece of cloth or uproot a plant. The author means that Yahweh forcibly removed them from their land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh has forcibly removed them from their land]
See how you translated the similar expression “in his nose” in verse 23.

Here Moses is speaking as if God had literally **thrown** the Israelites into another land. He means that God forcefully removed them from their homeland and sent them into exile. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and has forcefully sent them into another land]
